chapters.title: Chapter 4: The Post-2008 and Post-COVID Regimes

lessons.title: RBI's Response: The MPC, Repo Rate Hikes, and India's 2022-23 Inflation Fight

children.text: Recall the accountability clause from Chapter 3: if CPI inflation stays outside the RBI's 2% to 6% band for three consecutive quarters, the Monetary Policy Committee is legally required to write to the government explaining why, and what it will do about it. That clause sat unused for six years after the 2016 framework was created. In 2022, for the first time, the RBI actually had to use it.

body.text: The 2022-23 inflation fight was the first real stress test of India's post-2016 inflation-targeting framework, and it held. A rules-based, coordinated response across monetary and fiscal policy, not panic or denial, brought inflation back inside the band within about a year.

children.text: The Band Is Breached, and the Accountability Clause Triggers

India's CPI inflation crossed above the RBI's 6% upper tolerance band in early 2022 and stayed there through three consecutive quarters, driven heavily by the global shocks from the last lesson: elevated crude and edible oil prices, and the broader Russia-Ukraine commodity shock. Under the law you met in Chapter 3, that triggered the MPC's obligation to formally explain itself to the government, which it did around late 2022, attributing the miss substantially to these external, cost-push pressures rather than a domestic demand-pull failure. This is an important distinction: the accountability clause does not assume every miss is the RBI's fault, it forces a transparent explanation of which engine was actually responsible, exactly the diagnostic skill this course has been building from Chapter 1 onward.

events.title: CPI Breaches the Band
events.description: India's CPI crosses above 6%, the start of a three-quarter breach that will trigger the accountability clause.

events.title: An Off-Cycle Emergency Hike
events.description: In an unscheduled move between regular meetings, signalling urgency, the RBI raises the repo rate by 40 basis points to 4.40% and raises the Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR) by 50 basis points, draining liquidity from the banking system alongside the rate move.

events.title: Government Acts on the Fiscal Side
events.description: The government cuts excise duty on petrol and diesel to directly ease pump prices, and bans wheat exports to protect domestic food supply after the war disrupted global grain markets, both non-monetary tools working alongside the RBI.

events.title: The Hiking Cycle Continues
events.description: The MPC raises the repo rate at each subsequent scheduled meeting through the year, taking it from 4.40% toward 6.25% by December 2022.

events.title: Rates Reach Their Peak
events.description: The repo rate reaches 6.50%, a cumulative rise of about 250 basis points from where the cycle started, and the RBI holds there for an extended period as inflation gradually eases back toward the band.

children.text: Beyond the Repo Rate: A Coordinated Response

A pure interest-rate response makes most sense against demand-pull pressure. Since a meaningful share of the 2022 inflation was cost-push, imported energy and food costs, the government and the RBI reached for tools beyond the repo rate too. Cutting fuel excise duty put money directly back into consumers' hands at the pump without needing the slow transmission lag from Chapter 1. Banning wheat exports was a direct supply-side intervention, protecting domestic food availability rather than trying to cool demand for wheat that was not actually the problem. Together with the CRR hike tightening banking-system liquidity, this was a genuinely coordinated, multi-tool response, not a single-lever reaction.

cells: Overall demand and credit growth economy-wide
Excess liquidity in the banking system
Immediate pump-price relief, bypassing the monetary transmission lag
Domestic food availability, direct rather than demand-side

body.title: Match the Tool to the Engine
body.scenario: India's 2022 response combined an off-cycle repo hike, a CRR hike, a fuel excise duty cut, and a wheat export ban, all within about the same month.
body.prompt: For each of these four tools, identify whether it is primarily designed to cool demand-pull pressure, blunt a cost-push shock directly, or do something else entirely (such as managing liquidity or signalling credibility). What does the mix itself tell you about how policymakers had actually diagnosed this inflation episode?
body.modelAnswer: The repo hike targets demand-pull pressure economy-wide, the classic textbook lever. The CRR hike is a liquidity tool, tightening the plumbing of the banking system rather than directly targeting any single price. The fuel excise cut and the wheat export ban are not demand tools at all, they are direct interventions on the cost-push side, one easing a cost consumers already faced, the other protecting supply rather than trying to shrink demand. The mix itself is the tell: if policymakers believed this was purely a demand-pull problem, a rate hike alone would have been the whole response. Reaching for fiscal and administrative tools alongside it shows they had correctly diagnosed a blended regime, echoing the multi-engine read from the last lesson, and matched their tools to the actual mechanism rather than defaulting to the one lever central banks usually reach for first.

body.text: The RBI's own accountability report leaned heavily on this same diagnosis: it attributed most of the target miss to global, cost-push factors, elevated crude and edible oil prices, and the war's commodity shock, rather than to a failure of domestic demand management. Whether or not you find that framing fully convincing, it is a genuinely different conversation from the 1970s Fed simply calling inflation "somebody else's problem" and doing little about it. Here, the diagnosis came with a coordinated, multi-tool response attached.

children.text: A Coda: The Tomato Price Flare-Up

In July and August 2023, tomato prices in several Indian cities spiked well beyond ₹200 a kilogram after unseasonal rains hit key growing states, briefly pushing headline CPI back up even as the broader inflation fight had largely succeeded. If this sounds familiar, it should: it is almost exactly the quiz scenario from the very first lesson of this course, a narrow, volatile food component spiking while the underlying regime had genuinely calmed down. Winning the big structural fight against a 2022-style inflation regime does not retire the skill from Lesson 1. It just means you will keep needing it, on a smaller scale, indefinitely.

body.title: Quick Check
body.question: What does India's 2022-23 inflation fight demonstrate about the post-2016 inflation-targeting framework from Chapter 3?
options: That the accountability clause has never actually been used in practice
That the framework only works against demand-pull inflation and failed completely in 2022
That the framework held up under its first real stress test, forcing a transparent explanation and prompting a coordinated, multi-tool response rather than denial or delay
That India abandoned inflation targeting entirely in response to the 2022 shock
body.explanation: Far from failing, the framework did what it was designed to do: it forced transparency when the target was missed, and it coincided with a genuinely coordinated policy response rather than the kind of prolonged denial that let the 1970s US inflation become entrenched.

points: India's CPI breached the RBI's 6% band for three consecutive quarters in 2022, triggering the accountability clause from Chapter 3 for the first time since the 2016 framework began.
The RBI raised the repo rate by a cumulative ~250 basis points, from 4.00% to 6.50%, including a rare off-cycle emergency hike in May 2022.

The government paired this with fiscal and administrative tools, a fuel excise duty cut and a wheat export ban, correctly matching tools to a diagnosis of blended demand and cost-push pressure rather than relying on interest rates alone.

The July-August 2023 tomato price flare-up is a direct callback to Lesson 1 of this course: even after a major regime is tamed, narrow food-price shocks keep recurring, and the headline-versus-regime skill remains permanently relevant.

You now have the full historical toolkit, three engines, leading indicators, and five real regimes across a century. The final chapter turns this into a practical framework for what to actually hold, and how to read the next shift, as an investor.
